questions.q: Ask the user for five whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a list as whole numbers and display the list itself, in the form [8, 3, 5, 1, 9].

teach.say: A list holds many values in one variable. Start with an empty list and .append() each value onto the end of it.

brief: Keep them in the order they were typed, and print nothing else.
questions.starter: # Read five numbers into a list, then print the list

tests.why: The list has to keep the order the numbers were typed in.
Repeats are allowed - a list keeps every item, even when two are the same.
If you got ['30', '5', '100', '5', '12'] with quote marks you stored the text from input() instead of turning it into a number with int().

questions.fb: Start with an empty list and .append() each number as you read it - printing the list shows the square brackets and commas for you.

questions.q: Ask the user for how many colours there are and then that many colours, one on each line. Store them in a list and display [how many], then [last colour] on the next line.
brief: Print nothing but those two lines.
questions.starter: # Read the colours into a list, then report on it

tests.why: len() counts the items; the last one is at position len - 1, not len.
With one colour the first item is also the last - colours[1] is already past the end of the list.
The count must come from len(), not from printing the number you read at the start - they only match if every colour was appended.

questions.fb: len(list) tells you how many items there are, so the highest position you can read is len(list) - 1.

questions.q: Ask the user for four words, one on each line, and then a position counting from 0. Store the words in a list and display [the word at that position] and nothing else.

teach.say: A list is indexed like a string. box[0] is the first item and box[len(box) - 1] is the last.

brief: Only that one word is printed.
questions.starter: # Read four words, then print the one at the position given

tests.why: Position 2 is the third item, because the counting starts at 0.
Position 0 is the first item. Printing hammer means you used position 1 for the first item.
Four items means the last position is 3, not 4 - adding 1 would run off the end of the list.
Different words this time, so a program that prints a word you typed in yourself will fail here.

questions.fb: A list of four items has positions 0 to 3, so the last position is always one less than the length.

questions.q: Ask the user for five whole numbers, one on each line, then two positions counting from 0. Display [number at the first position], [number at the second position] and [their total], one on each line.
brief: The numbers go in a list, and nothing else is printed.
questions.starter: # Read five numbers, then look two of them up and add them

tests.why: Read the positions in the order the brief gives them - swapping them swaps the first two lines.
0 is the first number and 4 is the last of five. If either came out wrong you are counting the positions from 1.
The same position twice is allowed: the number is simply used twice, so the total is double it.
Add the two numbers you looked up, not the two position numbers - those would give 4.

questions.fb: Looking an item up with nums[a] gives you an ordinary number, which you can use in a sum like any other.

questions.q: Ask the user for four words, one on each line. Store them in a list and display a line for each, in the form [word] [how many letters it has].

teach.say: A for loop over a list hands you each item in turn, so you never need a position number for this job.

brief: One line per word, in the order they were typed.
questions.starter: # Read four words, then print each one with its length

tests.why: One line per plant, name first and length second, in the typed order.
Four lines even when every length is the same - the loop must run once for every item.
If you only got one line you printed after the loop instead of inside it - check the indentation.

questions.fb: A for loop over a list hands you the items one at a time, so you never need a position number for this job.

questions.q: Ask the user for five whole numbers, one on each line. Store them in a list and display a line for each, in the form [position] [number], with the positions counting from 0.

teach.say: range(len(box)) counts the positions of a list, so box[i] is the item the loop is on.

brief: One line per number, in the order they were typed.
questions.starter: # Loop over the positions, not the items

tests.why: The first line must be 0 7. If it says 1 7 you started counting the positions at 1.
With all five numbers the same, only the positions change - this is the clearest check that they run 0 to 4.
range(len(nums)) gives 0 up to 4 for five items - range(1, len(nums)) would miss the first one.

questions.fb: range(len(nums)) counts the positions, so nums[i] is the item at the position the loop is on.

questions.q: Ask the user for four items and then two more, one on each line. Append the last two onto the list of the first four. Display [how many items now], then every item, one on each line.
brief: Append onto that same list, in order - do not build a second one.
questions.starter: # Four items, then two more on the end

tests.why: .append() puts an item on the end, so the last two come after salt in the order they were typed.
The count comes from len() after both appends - four plus two is six, not four.
If an item is missing you replaced the list with the new value instead of appending to it.

questions.fb: basket.append(x) changes the list you already have, so there is nothing to assign it back to.

questions.q: Ask the user for five names, then a name to remove and a position counting from 0, one on each line. Take out that name, then delete the item now at that position. Display [each remaining name], one on each line.

teach.say: queue.remove(v) takes out the value v and del queue[i] takes out the item at position i. Each one makes the list shorter straight away.

brief: The position applies to the shortened list, after the named person has gone.
questions.starter: # One name out by value, one by position

tests.why: Once Cai has gone, position 0 is Ama. If Bo disappeared instead you counted the positions from 1.
The position counts along the shortened list. Deleting from the original five would have taken Cai instead of Dara.
Four names are left after the remove, so 3 is the last position - this is where going one too far crashes.
.remove() is given a name and del is given a position - mixing the two up is the usual slip here.

questions.fb: .remove() is given the value to take out; del is given the position. Both shorten the list at once, so the second one works on what is left.

questions.q: Ask the user for five whole numbers, one on each line. Display [total], then [average] on the next line, rounded to 1 decimal place, so 5 shows as 5.0.

teach.say: len(nums) is how many items a list holds, so dividing the total by it gives an average that works for any list. / always gives a real number.

brief: Divide the total by how many the list holds, and print nothing else.
questions.starter: # Total the list, then work out the average

tests.why: The average is the total divided by how many numbers there are. It must show one decimal place, so 5.0 and not 5.
Round to one decimal place with round(total / 5, 1) - printing the raw division gives 10.2 here but a long run of digits for other data.
If the total is right but the average is not, check you divided by 5 and not by 4.
All zeros should still work - a running total that starts at 0 handles this, one that starts at the first number does too, but one that starts at 1 does not.

questions.fb: Start the running total at 0 before the loop, add each item inside the loop, and divide only once the loop has finished.

questions.q: Ask the user for seven whole numbers, one on each line. Find the largest and the smallest with a loop of your own, not with max() or min(), and display [largest], then [smallest] on the next line.
brief: The numbers may be negative, and may all be the same.
questions.starter: # Find the largest and the smallest yourself

tests.why: Largest first, smallest second - printing them the other way round is the easiest mark to lose here.
When every number is the same it is both the largest and the smallest, so your comparisons must use > and < and not >= and <= in a way that breaks.
All seven are negative. Starting largest at 0 would wrongly report 0, so start it at the first item in the list instead.
The largest and the smallest are both near the start - a loop that begins at position 1 would skip the 50 entirely.

questions.fb: Start both answers at the first item, then compare every item against them in turn - the first item is the only safe starting guess.
forbid: The point of this question is the loop - find the largest yourself rather than using max().
The point of this question is the loop - find the smallest yourself rather than using min().

questions.q: Ask the user for eight marks out of 20, one on each line. Display [total], then [average] to 1 decimal place, then [how many are 12 or more], then [position of the highest mark], one on each line.
brief: Positions count from 0, and the earlier mark wins a tie.
questions.starter: # Total, average, passes, and where the best mark sits

tests.why: Four lines in the order the brief gives. The highest mark 20 is the third one, which is position 2 - position 3 means you counted from 1.
Nothing reaches 12, so the count of passes is 0 - a counter must start at 0 and be printed even when nothing was counted.
Two marks are 20. The brief asks for the first of them, position 1, so compare with > and not >= when you update the best position.
A mark of exactly 12 counts as a pass, so the answer is 4 - if you got 0 you used > 12 instead of >= 12.
The highest mark is the very last one, position 7 - a loop that stops one short of the end never sees it.

questions.fb: Four separate jobs over the same list: one running total, one counter with a condition, and one remembered position that you keep updating.
forbid: Find the highest mark with a loop of your own rather than using max().
Find the position of the highest mark as you go rather than looking it up with .index().
